newsReadings.title: When the Sky Stood Still: America's Four-Hour Ground Stop
newsReadings.passage:
On Friday afternoon, 13 November, air travel across the United States came to an almost complete standstill. At around 3:44 p.m. Eastern Time, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop, instructing every departing aircraft in the country to remain on the ground. It was the first such order since January 2023, and only the second nationwide ground stop since the attacks of 11 September 2001. For more than four hours, the busiest airspace in the world was effectively frozen.

The trouble began shortly before the order was issued. At 3:36 p.m., the FAA detected instability in its telecommunications network, and controllers at facilities across the country reported that their radio frequencies were "going in and out", forcing them to switch repeatedly between primary systems and backups. As many as 17 of the agency's 22 air route traffic control centres were affected, although none of them, officials stressed, "actually went dark". Because the agency could not immediately explain why so many facilities were failing at once, it took the most cautious course available and halted departures altogether. At the time, more than 3,500 aircraft were already airborne. Following established procedures, pilots and controllers brought every one of them down safely, and by 8 p.m. fewer than 400 aircraft remained in the sky.

The cause, according to the Department of Transportation, lay in routine maintenance work that had gone badly wrong. A long-standing FAA contractor, L3Harris, had been upgrading the ageing telecommunications system that links air traffic control facilities, replacing decades-old copper wire with fibre-optic cable at a remote location. Something in that work, officials said, caused a newly installed router to flood the network with traffic, disrupting communications and radar feeds. The defective equipment was isolated within 45 minutes, but the damage to the day's schedule was already done. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described the episode bluntly: "This was an FAA system that didn't meet the moment."

The disruption was enormous in scale. During the four and a half hours of the stop, more than 20,000 flights had been scheduled, and roughly 12,000 of them were affected in some way. According to flight-tracking data, nearly 6,000 flights were cancelled on Saturday and more than 6,400 delayed, while the FAA estimated that as many as 5,000 of the 41,000 flights scheduled for Saturday alone would be cancelled as airlines struggled to reposition aircraft and crews. Around 1.5 million passengers saw their plans upended, with long queues and crowded terminals at major hubs including Atlanta, Chicago O'Hare, New York's JFK and Dallas-Fort Worth. Although the ground stop was lifted at 8:15 p.m. on Friday, officials warned that the ripple effects would continue through the weekend, just weeks before the busy Thanksgiving travel season.

For all the alarm it caused, officials were quick to rule out the explanations that many had feared. Both the Transportation Secretary and the FAA Administrator, Bryan Bedford, stressed that there was "zero evidence" of a cyberattack, foreign interference or anything related to artificial intelligence. The failure, they insisted, was mundane rather than malicious: old equipment, stressed by new technology, had simply broken.

That ordinariness may be the most troubling part of the story. The copper-wire network at the heart of the failure is being phased out, but around 30 per cent of the lines have yet to be replaced, and the modernisation programme has been running for decades. Bedford acknowledged that the ageing technology "will continue to break until we replace it", a warning that turns a single afternoon of chaos into a question about how long a country can keep patching the infrastructure on which millions of journeys depend. Airlines, meanwhile, must rebuild trust as well as timetables, with the year's busiest travel week now only days away. The skies are open again, but the system that guards them remains, in the FAA's own admission, a work in progress.

newsReadings.title: A Dead Star's Clockwork Flash — and a Companion Like Our Sun
newsReadings.source: Phys.org / The Conversation, 14 November 2026; Nature Astronomy
newsReadings.passage:
Since 2022, astronomers have been puzzling over a strange new class of cosmic object. Known as long-period radio transients, these objects send out bright flashes of radio waves every few minutes to every few hours, then fall silent again. They do not fit neatly into any established category of star, and until recently nobody could say with confidence what produced them. New research published in the journal Nature Astronomy has now identified a surprising source for one of them: a dead star locked in orbit around a companion remarkably like our own Sun.

The discovery began in late 2024, when researchers using the Murchison Widefield Array radio telescope in Western Australia picked up a signal that repeated with extraordinary regularity. Short bursts of radio waves were arriving like clockwork every 7.9 minutes. The signal was found with a search method developed by doctoral student Csanad Horvath, and it stood out at once: nothing in the catalogue of known objects behaved quite like this.

Yet the pattern was stranger still. The pulses appeared only during a window of about six hours, followed by roughly 26 hours of silence. The most natural explanation, the team concluded, was that the source is a binary system: two stars circling each other once every 32 hours, with the radio pulses visible only when the geometry of the orbit brings the pulsing object into view. When the astronomers traced the signal back to its precise location in the sky, they found the source sitting exactly on top of a G-type star, a star of almost the same mass and temperature as the Sun.

That was the real surprise. An earlier long-period transient had been traced to a red dwarf, a small, cool star, probably orbiting a white dwarf, the dense remnant left behind when a star like the Sun exhausts its fuel. This time, however, the companion was not a dim red dwarf but a star much like our own. The researchers believe the pulsing object is a white dwarf pulsar, the first of its kind ever found in orbit around a Sun-like star. In such a system, the white dwarf's powerful magnetic field sweeps beams of radio waves across space as it spins, rather like a lighthouse, and we detect a flash each time a beam points towards Earth.

The finding matters for several reasons. First, it shows that these enigmatic broadcasters are not confined to one type of stellar partnership; they can arise in very different settings, which means astronomers will need to broaden their search. Second, it demonstrates how much remains hidden in data that telescopes have already collected. The Murchison Widefield Array had been scanning the sky for years, and the signal was there all along, waiting for a sharper method to pull it out of the noise.

There is also a wider lesson about how science advances. The white dwarf in this system is, by any ordinary measure, dead: it has burned through its fuel and collapsed to a fraction of its former size. Yet paired with a living, Sun-like companion, it produces one of the most regular and conspicuous signals in the radio sky. Each new detection also sharpens the picture of stellar evolution, showing how the remnants of dead stars can remain among the most precise timekeepers in the universe. The result, reported by Samuel J. McSweeney and colleagues, hints that many more such systems may be waiting to be found, and that the quietest corners of the sky may turn out to be the most talkative. As survey telescopes grow more sensitive, astronomers expect the census of these clockwork objects to grow, and with it, our understanding of how stars live, die and, in rare and remarkable cases, keep on shining.
